What is the kinetic energy of the cannon ball at the top of its trajectory?

A $E\cos\theta$
B $E\sin^2\theta$
C $E\cos^2\theta$
D $E$

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify the surviving velocity component and square it in the kinetic-energy ratio.
questions.misconception: Scaling kinetic energy linearly with speed

explanation.body: At the top, the vertical velocity is zero and the speed is $u\cos\theta$, where $u$ is the launch speed. The kinetic-energy ratio is $\frac{\tfrac12m(u\cos\theta)^2}{\tfrac12mu^2}=\cos^2\theta$, so the kinetic energy there is $E\cos^2\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the horizontal speed factor without squaring it.
perOption.B: Uses the vertical launch component, which has fallen to zero at the top.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Keeps the full launch kinetic energy even though the vertical component of velocity has fallen to zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object is thrown vertically upwards in air. The times for the upward motion $t_{\mathrm{u}}$ and the downward motion $t_{\mathrm{d}}$ to return to the same height are compared.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: An object is thrown vertically upwards in air. The times for the upward motion tu and the downward motion td to return to the same height are compared. Which statement is correct? A $t_{\mathrm{d}}$ is greater because at a given speed the resultant force when the object is moving downwards is smaller than the retarding force when it is moving upwards. B $t_{\mathrm{d}}$ is greater because the object moves faster on its downward motion and therefore the air resistance is greater. C $t_{\mathrm{u}}$ is greater because at a given speed, the resultant force when the object is moving downwards is greater than the retarding force when it is moving upwards. D $t_{\mathrm{u}}$ is greater because the object moves faster on its downward motion due to gravitational force acting in the same direction as its motion.

options.label: A
options.text: $t_{\mathrm{d}}$ is greater because at a given speed the resultant force when the object is moving downwards is smaller than the retarding force when it is moving upwards.

options.label: B
options.text: $t_{\mathrm{d}}$ is greater because the object moves faster on its downward motion and therefore the air resistance is greater.

options.label: C
options.text: $t_{\mathrm{u}}$ is greater because at a given speed, the resultant force when the object is moving downwards is greater than the retarding force when it is moving upwards.

options.label: D
options.text: $t_{\mathrm{u}}$ is greater because the object moves faster on its downward motion due to gravitational force acting in the same direction as its motion.

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must compare the direction of drag and the resulting acceleration on each leg.
questions.misconception: Assuming gravity makes the descent faster despite air resistance.

explanation.body: On the way up, both weight and air resistance act downward, so the object slows at a rate greater than $g$. On the way down, air resistance opposes weight, so the downward acceleration is less than $g$. Over the same height interval the descent therefore takes longer, so $t_{\mathrm d}>t_{\mathrm u}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Drag adds to weight during the ascent and opposes it during the descent.
perOption.B: At the same height the object is slower on the way down because drag has dissipated energy.
perOption.C: Reverses the force comparison because drag reduces the resultant on descent.
perOption.D: Ignores the upward drag during descent and incorrectly infers a shorter descent time.

questions.difficultyReason: Standard idea that projectile motion without air resistance is independent of mass.
questions.misconception: Heavier objects fall faster

explanation.body:
As air resistance is negligible, the acceleration ($g$) does not depend on mass, so it does not change.

If the pilot wants to score a direct hit, at which position should he release the bomb? A When the plane is $1010\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. B When the plane is $1270\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. C When the plane is $1390\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally. D When the plane is $1510\ \mathrm{m}$ away from the naval ship horizontally.

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A fighter bomber is travelling at 138 m s−1 horizontally at a height of 500 m above sea level. It is on a bombing run to its target, a naval ship which is movin

questions.difficultyReason: Combines time of fall with relative horizontal velocity of a moving target.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the target's motion or adding the velocities instead of subtracting

explanation.body:
Vertically the bomb starts with zero velocity: $500 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.81)t^2$, so $t = 10.1\ \mathrm{s}$ to reach sea level.

In that time the bomb moves $138 \times 10.1 = 1394\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally, while the ship moves $12 \times 10.1 = 121\ \mathrm{m}$ further away.

So the bomb must be released when the horizontal separation is $1394 - 121 \approx 1270\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the bomb's horizontal range minus the ship's motion incorrectly (too small a separation).
perOption.B: Correct. Bomb's horizontal range minus the distance the ship moves during the fall.
perOption.C: Ignores the ship's motion: this is just the bomb's horizontal range of about 1390 m.
perOption.D: Adds the ship's displacement instead of subtracting it, though the ship moves in the same direction as the bomb.

questions.stemText:
An object is launched with a speed of $50.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, as shown.

[Diagram: The launch velocity points diagonally upwards to the right at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. The launch and landing points are on level ground, $100\ \mathrm{m}$ apart.]

The ground is level. The object lands on the ground $100\ \mathrm{m}$ from its initial launch position.

What is the value of the angle $\theta$?

You may need to make use of the double angle formula: $\sin(2\theta)=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$

A  $2.8^\circ$
B  $5.5^\circ$
C  $11^\circ$
D  $79^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: An object is launched with a speed of 50.9 m s-1 at an angle θ above the horizontal, as shown. 50.9 m s-1 100 m The ground is level. The object lands on the gro

appearances.originalFile: grail:10439 CJC.H2.PRELIM.2023.P1.QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students eliminate flight time between two motion equations and solve a double-angle equation.
questions.misconception: Overlooking the complementary launch angle

explanation.body: The horizontal motion gives $50.9t\cos\theta=100$. Taking upwards as positive, the return to ground level gives $0=50.9t\sin\theta-\tfrac12(9.81)t^2$, so the nonzero flight time is $t=50.9\sin\theta/[\tfrac12(9.81)]$. Substituting into the horizontal equation and using the double-angle identity gives $100=50.9^2\sin(2\theta)/9.81$. The school takes the solution $2\theta\approx22^\circ$, giving $\theta\approx11^\circ$.

perOption.A: This launch angle gives a range of about 26 m.
perOption.B: This launch angle gives a range of about 50 m.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the lower-angle solution.
perOption.D: This is also valid to the stated precision, since complementary angles give the same range.

explanation.body: Take upward as positive and use $s_y=u_yt+\tfrac12a_yt^2$. Substitution gives $3.0-2.3=(6.5\sin50^\circ)t-\tfrac12(9.81)t^2$, so $4.905t^2-4.97929t+0.7=0$. questions.difficultyReason: Find the vertical and horizontal velocity components and combine them to obtain speed.
questions.misconception: Using the vertical component as the speed

explanation.body: Take upwards and rightwards as positive. Vertically, $v_y=u_y+a_yt=8.00+(-1.62)(9.00)=-6.58\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Horizontally, $v_x=u_x+a_xt=4.00+(0)(9.00)=4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed is $\sqrt{(-6.58)^2+(4.00)^2}=7.70\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising the ball still has horizontal KE at the top and estimating its fraction.
questions.misconception: Thinking KE is zero at the top of the trajectory

explanation.body: The total energy is the initial kinetic energy $E=\tfrac12mu^2$. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, but the constant horizontal velocity is $u\cos60^\circ=u/2$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m(u/2)^2=E/4$. perOption.C: Keeps kinetic energy above half the total, as for a launch below $45^\circ$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A double-ended launching device fires two identical steel balls X and Y at exactly the same time. The diagram shows the initial velocities of the balls. They are both launched horizontally, but Y has greater speed.

Which statement explains what an observer would see?
questions.stemText: A double-ended launching device fires two identical steel balls X and Y at exactly the same time. The diagram shows the initial velocities of the balls. They are both launched horizontally, but Y has greater speed. Which statement explains what an observer would see? A X reaches the ground before Y, because X lands nearer to the launcher. B Y reaches the ground before X, because Y has greater initial speed. C Both X and Y reach the ground simultaneously, because gravitational acceleration is the same for both. D Both X and Y reach the ground simultaneously, because air resistance will cause both to have the same final speed.

options.label: A
options.text: X reaches the ground before Y, because X lands nearer to the launcher.

options.label: B
options.text: Y reaches the ground before X, because Y has greater initial speed.

options.label: C
options.text: Both X and Y reach the ground simultaneously, because gravitational acceleration is the same for both.

options.label: D
options.text: Both X and Y reach the ground simultaneously, because air resistance will cause both to have the same final speed.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14595 2024 TJC H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Classic independence of horizontal and vertical motion.
questions.misconception: Faster horizontal speed means shorter fall time

explanation.body: Both balls are launched horizontally from the same height, so each has zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration $g$. Their vertical motion is identical and independent of the horizontal motion, so the time to fall is the same: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$. They land together; Y simply travels farther horizontally.

perOption.A: Landing nearer does not mean landing earlier; fall time depends only on height.
perOption.B: Horizontal speed does not affect the time of fall.
perOption.C: Correct. Same height and same $g$ give the same fall time.
perOption.D: Air resistance is neglected in the intended reasoning, and the final speeds would differ anyway (Y is faster horizontally).

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object of mass 0.40 kg is projected into the air and follows a curved path above horizontal ground.

The object takes a time of 1.5 s to move along its path. The object lands a horizontal distance of 18 m from its initial position. Air resistance is negligible.

What is the kinetic energy of the object at its maximum height ?
questions.stemText: An object of mass 0.40 kg is projected into the air and follows a curved path above horizontal ground. The object takes a time of 1.5 s to move along its path. The object lands a horizontal distance of 18 m from its initial position. Air resistance is negligible. What is the kinetic energy of the object at its maximum height ? A 0 J B 2.4 J C 11 J D 29 J

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires obtaining the horizontal speed from the range and then calculating the kinetic energy at the apex.
questions.misconception: Assuming all velocity components vanish at the apex

explanation.body: The horizontal velocity is constant, with $u_x=18/1.5=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so $E_{\mathrm k}=\tfrac12 m u_x^2=\tfrac12(0.40)(12)^2=28.8\ \mathrm{J}$, or $29\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Treats zero vertical velocity at the apex as zero total velocity.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal speed without squaring it in the kinetic energy formula.
perOption.C: Uses the launch vertical speed of about $7.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in place of the horizontal speed at the apex.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows the trajectory of a projectile and the velocity $v$ of the projectile at point P in its trajectory. P is located before the projectile reaches the peak altitude. Air resistance acts on the projectile. The acceleration of the projectile at P is $a$.

[The dashed trajectory rises from left to right above a horizontal ground line. At P, the tangent velocity arrow $v$ points up and to the right.]

What are the magnitudes of the horizontal component and the vertical component of the acceleration of the projectile at P?

Horizontal component of $a$ | Vertical component of $a$
A Zero | Greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
B Non-zero | Greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
C Zero | $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
D Non-zero | $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires resolving the drag force and combining its vertical component with weight.
questions.misconception: Applying the no-drag acceleration components when drag is present

explanation.body: At P, the drag force acts opposite to the upward and forward velocity, so it has a horizontal component and a downward component. The horizontal acceleration is therefore non-zero. The downward component of drag adds to the weight, making the vertical acceleration greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ in magnitude.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal component of drag.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the acceleration components for a projectile with negligible air resistance.
perOption.D: Includes the horizontal drag but omits the downward component of drag.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An eagle is flying horizontally at 6.00 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ with a fish in its claws. It accidentally drops the fish.

How much time passes before the fish’s speed doubles? Neglect air resistance.
questions.stemText: An eagle is flying horizontally at 6.00 m s−1 with a fish in its claws. It accidentally drops the fish. How much time passes before the fish’s speed doubles? Neglect air resistance. A 0.500 s B 1.06 s C 2.12 s D 4.00 s

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The final speed must be resolved into components before using the vertical motion equation.
questions.misconception: Treating gravity as an acceleration along the velocity

explanation.body: The final speed is $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, with horizontal component $v_x=6.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. From $v_x^2+v_y^2=12^2$, we get $36+v_y^2=144$, giving a downward component of $10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Using $v_y=u_y+at$ downwards gives $10.4=0+9.81t$, so $t=1.06\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Treats the increase in total speed as the vertical velocity gained, underestimating the time.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Doubles the time obtained from the vertical velocity gain.
perOption.D: Overestimates the time required for gravity to build the vertical component to $10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two coins are projected from a horizontal table at the same initial speed $u$.
Coin X is projected horizontally.
Coin Y is projected upwards at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.

Both coins hit the horizontal ground without bouncing.
Assume the air resistance on each coin is negligible.
Which statement about the motion of the coins is correct?

A Both coins hit the ground with the same speed.
B Both coins travel the same vertical distance.
C Coin Y hits the ground before coin X.
D Coin Y has a smaller vertical acceleration.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires relating impact speed to energy while distinguishing vertical distance from displacement.
questions.misconception: Assuming launch direction changes impact speed.

explanation.body: Both coins start with the same speed and fall through the same net height. By conservation of energy, they gain the same kinetic energy per unit mass and therefore hit the ground with the same speed.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Y rises before falling, so it travels a greater vertical distance.
perOption.C: Y takes longer to reach the ground because it initially moves upwards.
perOption.D: With negligible air resistance, both coins have the same downward acceleration.
